111c8317df: Build00:20–00:55 Part 1: Where the guitar came from
c9193f8900: From the oud of the Middle East all the way to Spain
5265cad37d: Early guitars had strings in pairs, pressed and plucked together, a bit like today's 12-string guitar. Four courses means eight strings.
47ccb8238b: The vihuela and five-course guitar thrived most in Spain, and the classical guitar is still called the "Spanish guitar" today.
16941c28f9: In the late 18th century the paired strings became six single strings, and the tuning settled on today's E A D G B E.
162e515287: BuildPart 2: How the guitar changed (1)
c9ca5d303f: The highs and lows of the classical guitar
ed6d030723: The four-course guitar used gut strings. The five-course guitar appeared in the 16th century and gradually replaced it.
b09554b5b2: The five-course guitar was popular at court and among ordinary people, often accompanying singing and dancing; the lute slowly left the stage.
8e54adb152: The six-string guitar takes shape. Sor, Aguado and Carcassi left a large body of pieces and method books.
5aab863886: The piano took centre stage and fewer and fewer composers wrote for guitar. Tárrega brought the guitar back to audiences through his playing and arrangements.
e798f5481b: The piano was loud, could play melody and harmony at once, and suited big concert halls; guitars of the time were quiet and hard to hear in a hall. "Not loud enough" comes up again and again in the guitar's history.
d38ff04521: BuildPart 2: How the guitar changed (2)
d14da07908: For more volume: classical, folk and electric guitars
bbbd7d152b: Spanish luthier Torres enlarged the body, set the string length at about 65 cm and used fan bracing, establishing what the classical guitar looks like today.
65b7c3183c: Segovia championed it all his life, and Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez put the classical guitar on the concerto stage.
0e873d55a9: Blues, country and folk rose in America. Martin switched to higher-tension steel strings and strengthened the body for a brighter, louder sound.
9e39cd6971: Pickups turn string vibration into an electrical signal that an amp can make louder. In 1950 Leo Fender released a mass-produced solid-body electric guitar.
d3962ced2f: For three hundred years, nearly every change to the guitar has been about volume, so the guitar can be heard clearly in a band.

69f744de84: BuildPart 3: Parts of the guitar
2fdea6c95e: Once you pluck a string, which parts does the sound pass through?
1de2c07295: The air bounces back and forth inside the body, grows louder, and finally comes out of the sound hole. That's why the top and body wood affect the tone most.
3633538efe: Which part goes in the question-mark box?
9398a9b504: The other end of the string rests on the saddle, which sits in the bridge, which is glued to the top, so the vibration travels all the way into the top. The nut is at the neck end and sets the string spacing.

dbb6f4575b: Turn01:05–01:40 Part 3: What the body is made of
0dd5cddddf: Laminated and solid: both wood, each with its own tone
9a7a93637a: Look at the edge of the top through the sound hole: if the top and bottom layers are different colours with a layer in between, it's most likely laminated; if the grain runs through in one piece, it's solid.
67afb21649: A "solid top" means only the top is solid; "all solid" means the sides and back are solid too.
f11a7bb68d: The body wood decides the tone, resonance and volume. Choosing a guitar within your budget with sensible materials that's easy to press is more practical than chasing the finest wood.
ea0c96a77a: Common woods: each has its own colour and its own tone
b6bc7195ee: Pale yellow and hard. A bright, clear sound; the most common top on folk guitars.
fd00a9e315: Dark orange-brown and soft. A warm, round sound that vibrates easily; often used on classical guitars.
e79e770268: Thick, warm mids and a focused tone; great for playing and singing.
9d401a54d2: Deep lows, bright highs and rich overtones, with a sense of space.
1414d5795f: Hard and light, with a clean, direct sound that doesn't get buried by other instruments in a band.
7fa65bedae: From Hawaii; the more it's played, the sweeter it sounds, with lovely upper mids.
d6072eec2c: Between mahogany and rosewood, a balanced, warm sound.

48cbe338a1: TurnChoosing and caring for a guitar
23f441094e: Put steel strings on a classical guitar and it gets louder
b05e1c6d4e: MythSteel strings pull too hard for a classical guitar's neck and bridge, which will lift or warp.
f34fd9128b: The bigger the guitar, the better for beginners
07d3dfe641: MythChoose by your body size. If the body is too big your right arm can't wrap around it, and your shoulder will hurt after a while.
e5cb0d3e62: Folk guitars are louder than classical guitars
d0a4fe8f47: FactHigher-tension steel strings plus X bracing give a bright, loud sound.
9b5d391a30: Solid-wood guitars sound better the more you play them
4bef669439: FactA single piece of wood vibrating over years sounds more and more open; laminates change less.
913f3596b2: If pressing hurts your fingers, the guitar is broken
1595b762ca: MythSore fingertips for the first two weeks are normal; if the action at string 6, fret 12 is over about 3 mm, have a technician adjust it.
9a2e7e75fc: It's fine to leave the guitar in the car or in the sun by a window after playing
858f9a1fa6: MythHeat and humidity make wood swell or crack. Keep it in its bag out of the sun, and dehumidify in Taiwan's summers.
